admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act.

of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not.

calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry.

and 25H of the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 01.04.2017 and he was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated 
that his salary used to be credited in his bank account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which his salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman.

permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent 10.1 being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of 
his appointment by respondent 10.2 and has filed a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the 
workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 


12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing 
his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to 
perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 


Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are 
not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract 
basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be

inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In 
view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein 
admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 


Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in 
the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, 
salary, letter of appointment by respondent no.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature 
for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally 
lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P 
Singh in his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the 
conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to 
the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. 
Ex.R-2 is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges 
that workman was paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 
10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was 
supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent 10.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) 
of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G 
and 25H of the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 05.07.2015 and he was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated 
that his salary used to be credited in his bank account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which his salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. 
However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from 
the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis 
were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of 
respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.1 as has been discussed above. There does not exist any relationship

of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of 
employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as 
regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the 
workman. Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by 
respondent 10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement 
executed between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions 
of AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry 
was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that 
workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and 
no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not 
mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a 
department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is 
provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of 
respondent no.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent 10.2 (contractor) is currently not 
working with respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary 
given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, 
this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of 
compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


ii. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 


iii. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 05.07.2015 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (More than 2 years 
and less than 5 years), so he is entitled for Rs.30,000/-. 


25. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.30,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the 
date of award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai 
karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.

of the Act.

The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. B.-ALC©-I/8/(15)2023-B-2 dated 
23/10/2024 passed in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2A) of 
Section 10 of the Industrial Dispute Act 1947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as 
under: 


“Whether the termination of service of Shri Ashok Dayashankar Tripathi by M/s Vishal Enterprises, 
Contracotr of M/s. HPCL Auto Care Centre(T&E) is legal and justified? If not, what relief the workman is 
entitled to?” ” 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (1) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“Tt is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (7), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; 


The Second party workmen by its application dated 01.04.2025 desired to withdraw the present dispute and prayed 
that the second party workmen be allowed to withdraw the dispute. 


[भाग त--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2361 
The application is allowed. As such the reference is disposed of for want of prosecution. 

For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the workman is not entitled for any relief. 

Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid. 


Award as above.

In support of claim statement, petitioner has filed Chief statement affidavit of WWI and also filed 
photocopies of the document. On the other hand, Respondent has filed Chief affidavit of the witness MW1. 


Heard the argument of learned counsel for either parties. 
Ongoing pleading of both the parties following issues emerged for determination in the present case: - 


1. Whether the action of management of Airport director, Begumpet Airport, Hyderabad, in changing the 
service condition of the workman, Shri Mohammad Ghouse, Senior Assistant Lift, is legal and justifiable? 


2. Whether the petitioner is entitled to the relief claimed? 
Findings: - 
Issue No.I:- 


In support of the averment made in the claim statement, petitioner in oral evidence has submitted his own 
Chief statement affidavit and therein he has reiterated the averment made in the claim statement. Petitioner witness 
was cross-examined by the Respondent Counsel and in cross-examination WW1 has stated that it is true that in chief 
examination he has not marked any document, although he has submitted list of documents along with the claim 
statement. Further, witness admits that it is true that he has not mentioned what service conditions have been changed 
by the Respondent. Further, in reply to the question by the Respondent that what changes of service condition made 
by the Respondent the Petitioner witness WW1 state that at the Airport, its employees working as shift-duty round the 
clock 24/7 as on today continuing in Begumpet Airport without change of any salary, workplace, or overtime 
allowances. Further, witness states that it is true that whenever worker is working overtime, Respondent used to pay 
the overtime wages. Further, witness states that at Begumpet Airport, VIPs and commercial flights are coming and 
landing. Further, witness state that it is not true to suggest that Respondent is not extracting overtime and night work 
from the workers, and that they are not entitled to any allowances. It is not true to suggest that there is no change of 
service condition due to the change of Airport from Begumpet to Shamshabad. 


Thus, petitioner has failed to substantiate his claim by oral or documentary evidence about the change in the 
service condition due to shifting of the commercial flights from the Begumpet Airport to Shamshabad Airport. 
Further, petitioner has failed to specify and establish by evidence that what are those service conditions of the 
Petitioner that has been changed to the prejudice of the interest of the Petitioner. Petitioner failed to produce any oral 
or documentary evidence on record in support of his claim about change in service condition. However, Petitioner 
witness has admitted in cross examination that they are doing the same work and are being paid as in the past. 


Moreover, Respondent has filed chief statement affidavit of the witness MW1, wherein the witness has 
reiterated the contention made in the counter. This witness was cross-examined by the petitioner and in his cross- 
examination, witness states that, due to official requirement, only one lift is in use for the terminal building, and the 


[भाग त----खण्ड 301)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2365 


technical block lift is working till date for operational purposes. Further, Respondent witness state that it is not true to 
say that even today ATC works around the clock but work only for operational requirements. Furthermore, MW1 
states that it is not true that the petitioner has illegally transferred and changed his service condition, but his transfer 
was on administrative grounds. Further, suggestion was given to the witness that only support the rival union, 
petitioner has been transferred to Rajmundry has been denied by the witness. Further, witness state that at Rajmundry 
there is no lift, but a conveyor belt post exists at the Rajmundry airport. 


Thus, on appreciation of evidence of by either parties, I am constrained to come to conclusion that the 
petitioner has failed to substantiate his claim of a change in his service condition. However, the petitioner Sri. Gouse 
Mohd has attained the age of superannuation on 30. 06.2014 and retired and has settled all his claims with 
Respondent Management. Therefore, claim of the Petitioner has become infructuous as no cause of action survives on 
account of his retirement, and no relief could be granted to the petitioner. Thus, petitioner had attained the age of 
superannuation on 307 June 2014 and has settled all his claims with the Respondent. Therefore, dispute relating to the 
petitioner's claim about change in service conditions anted dated 23" March 2008 has become infructuous and with 
retirement of Petitioner from service after attaining superannuation age, the employer-employee relationship between 
Petitioner and Respondent has come to an end and remedies of service law like change in service condition are 
generally prospective and tied to active service. Therefore, this court cannot typically order to be place in a specific 
active-duty post or reverse the past order as if the employer was still in service. 


Therefore, in view of the foregone discussion I am constrained to hold that the action of the Respondent 
management of the Airport director, Begumpet Airport, is legal and justified, as the petitioner failed to substantiate 
his claim regarding change in service condition. Further, due to retirement of Petitioner after attaining the age of 
superannuation on 30.06.2014. the cause of action with referred dispute does not service hence became infructuous. 
This issue is decided against the petitioner. 


Issue No. II: - 


In view of the discussion and findings given at point no. 1 Petitioner is not entitled to any relief and 
claim statement filed by the Petitioner deserved to be dismissed. 


AWARD 


The action of the management of Airport Director, Begumpet Airport Hyderabad is held legal and justified. The 
claim petition sans merit stands dismissed. Reference is answered accordingly.

Whether the departmental enquiry conducted against the workman is a just, proper and legal? 


Management filed and proved enquiry documents. They filed affidavit of its witness as his examination-in-chief. He 
has been cross-examined by Workman Side. 


The Workman filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief he has been cross-examined by management. 


On the basis of the arguments and record, preliminary issue was decided vide order dated 07.03.2025, holding the 
departmental enquiry just, legal and proper. This order is part of this Award. 


Following additional issues were framed thereafter:- 
1. Whether the charges have been rightly held proved from evidence in enquiry? 
2. Whether the punishment is proportionate to the charges? 
3. Whether the workman is entitled to any relief? 

No evidence was filed by any of the parties on additional issues. 


I have heard arguments of Learned Counsel Mr. Uttam Maheswari for Workman and Learned Counsel Mr. 
Neeraj Kewat for Management and have gone through the record. Management side has filed written submissions 
also which are part of record. I have gone through the written submissions as well. 


Additional Issue No.1, 
Charges against the workman have been detailed earlier. 


Case of management is that the workman first absented himself from 09.12.1999 till 11.07.2005 , he was issued 
a charge sheet dated 14.09.2005 in this respect and submitted his written explanation in this respect but he did not 
report on duty even thereafter till 11.12.2012, hence, repeated his misconduct which he had committed earlier. Thus, 
the fresh charge with respect to unauthorized absence from 2005 to 2012 was added in the charge sheet and enquiry 
proceeded. This pleading is supported from record. Hence, it cannot be said that the enquiry was initiated with 
unexplained inordinate delay. In total, the workman has been alleged to have absented himself from duty 
unauthorizedly and willfully without intimation or any leave sanctioned. 


Perusal of record of enquiry shows that regarding his absence from 1999 to 2005, the workman took a case that 
he was sick and had informed the management accordingly in his reply to the first charge sheet regarding his absence 
from 2005 to 2012, the workman took a case that he was ill for the said period also, his this defense taken during 
enquiry is not supported by medical evidence. 


The Enquiry Officer found during his enquiry that the workman was transferred in the year 1999 and since 
then he absented till 2012 and never reported on duty. It is also found during the enquiry that the establishment has its 
own medical facilities, having qualified doctors and good hospital. The workman was required to avail this facility 
which he did not. 


The settled proposition of law with respect to proof of charges in a departmental enquiry is that the charges 
need not be proved beyond reasonable doubt as they are required to be proved in a criminal trial. 


Testing the evidence during the enquiry on these parameters, the charges are held to have been rightly 
proved as recorded by the Enquiry Officer. 


Additional issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Additional Issue No. 2, 


The charges proved are unauthorized and wilful absence from workplace for 13 years. No employer can afford such 
an employee. Hence, the punishment of dismissal from service is held not disproportionate to the charge proved. 


Additional issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly. 
Additional Issue No. 3, 


On the basis of above discussion and findings, the workman is held entitled to no relief.

No other point was pressed. 
In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.- 
AWARD 


“The action of management, M.O.1.L. Limited in terminating the services of workman, Rajesh Bharatlal Nayak on 
the basis of charge sheet dated 18.06.2013 as mentioned in the reference, is held just, legal and proper and the 
workman is held entitled to no relief. ”

"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable

amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be

government within a period of not exceeding three month."

Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WWI in 
evidence and exhibited document W1 to W22. The evidence recorded in said petition may be treated as evidence of 
Petitioner in this case including cross examination of WW1. Since Petitioner has similar averment and evidence in 
both the petition. It is settled law that the rule of evidence Act do not apply strictly to the matter under I-D. Act.

13. Although Respondent has contended that all the wages and dues towards the final settlement have been paid 
to the Petitioner workman but in support of his contention Respondent has not filed any document to corroborate it. 
Respondent No. 1 has also examined witness MW2 Sri K. Sudhakar Rao who has produced and exhibited document 
Ex.M1 to Ex.M6 and states that Ex. M6 is showing the amount paid by 20 Respondent to claimants but in cross 
examination MW2 states that it is true that Ex.M6 relates to amount Rs. 28,58,522/- which is mentioned in para 5 of 
chief statement of MW1 and he is not aware that Rs. 61,76,628/- is still balance due to be paid to workman. Thus, the 
testimony of MW? is not direct evidence in respect of payment of claimed amount in the petition, hence his evidence 
is not relevant in this regard. Therefore, contention of the Respondent No.1 in this context is untenable for the want 
of cogent and relevant evidence. Thus, ongoing oral and documentary evidence on record, it is established that the 
Petitioner workman is entitled to receive from the employer Respondent No.3 the amount of Rs.83,444.92ps. for the 
period of August,2009 to 2012 towards retrenchment allowances as per document Ex. W12. 


14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its 
industry during the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 as contract labour engaged by Respondent No.3. Since the 
Respondent No. 3 was sub-contractor for labour supply for the work order Ex. W8 of Respondent No.2, therefore, 
Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 2" 
Respondent or 3™ Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the 
workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 
burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally. 


15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal

employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, ''(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment...". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 47 February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence

of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act, 1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for 
Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. ४४8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.l under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. 1 & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable.

18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. | as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 


ORDER 
The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 is allowed. 


Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant,

order Respondent No.1 is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of due 
1.e., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 


It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No. 3 the sub-contractor jointly and severally.

11. Perused the record. At the outset, Respondent counsel urged that present petition filed by the Petitioner for the 
recovery of full and final payment amounting to Rs.83,537.85ps. along with the interest for the work under contract is 
not maintainable under section 33-C(2) of ID Act 1947 as there is no amount due to the Petitioner from Respondent. 


Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable 
of being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the 
amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be 
wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month." 


Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is 
entitled to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. 
Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WWI in

is not relevant in this regard. Therefore, contention of the Respondent No.1 in this context is untenable for the want 
of cogent and relevant evidence. Thus, ongoing oral and documentary evidence on record, it is established that the 
Petitioner workman is entitled to receive from the employer Respondent No.3 the amount of Rs.83,537.85ps. for the 
period of August,2009 to 2012 towards retrenchment allowances as per document Ex. W12. 


14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its 
industry during the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 as contract labour engaged by Respondent No.3. Since the 
Respondent No. 3 was sub-contractor for labour supply for the work order Ex. W8 of Respondent No.2, therefore, 
Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 2" 
Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the 
workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 
burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally. 


15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."' In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal

employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 47 February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for

Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. W8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No. 3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer | the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1 industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. 1 & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
1०.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to

Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally.

ORDER 
The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 is allowed. 


Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam is directed to pay the amount of Rs. 83,537.85ps. to the Petitioner within 30 days from the date of this 
order Respondent No.1 is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of due 
1.e., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 


It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from

Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act

"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable 
of being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the 
amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be 
wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month." 


Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is

Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the

burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to

labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (व) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes ''(6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."' In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 3" September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2399 


that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 47 February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act, 1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for 
Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. ४४8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


2400 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 4, 2026/CHAITRA 14, 1948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 
(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. | has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. 1 & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. | as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 


ORDER 
The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 is allowed. 


Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam is directed to pay the amount of Rs. 83,073.23ps. to the Petitioner within 30 days from the date of this 
order Respondent No.1 is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of due 
1.e., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 


It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No. 3 the sub-contractor jointly and severally.
