19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.”

benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 


observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which

(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 


of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 

contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 

contained therein; or” 
Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 
17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (9५) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 
(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 
Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 


No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(1)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2610 


of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. 1 in this context is untenable. 

18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. | and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 

ORDER 

The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 is allowed. 

Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam is directed to pay the amount of Rs. 84,652.92ps. to the Petitioner within 30 days from the date of this 
order Respondent No.1! is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of due 
ie., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 

It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No. 3 the sub-contractor jointly and severally. 

Ordered accordingly.

(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 


Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


[भाग [avs 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/44 14, 1948 2624 


(०) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 

(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 

“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 

16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.”

11. Perused the record. At the outset, Respondent counsel urged that present petition filed by the Petitioner for the 
recovery of full and final payment amounting to Rs.83,259.08ps. along with the interest for the work under contract is 
not maintainable under section 33-C(2) of ID Act 1947 as there is no amount due to the Petitioner from Respondent. 


Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable 
of being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the 
amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be 
wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month." 


Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is 
entitled to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. 
Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WWI in 
evidence and exhibited document W1 to W22. The evidence recorded in said petition may be treated as evidence of

19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be

employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA

money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were

(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil

“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.”

is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 


powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not.

Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 

"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable of being 
computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the amount at 
which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be wait under this 
act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate government within a 
period of not exceeding three month." 

12. Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is 
entitled to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. 
Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WWI in 
evidence and exhibited document W1 to W22. The evidence recorded in said petition may be treated as evidence of 
Petitioner in this case including cross examination of WW1. Since Petitioner has similar averment and evidence in 
both the petition. It is settled law that rules of Evidence Act, are not strictly applicable to the matters under Industrial 
Dispute Act. Therefore, evidence produced by Petitioner in support of his claim is admissible. Therefore, evidence 
recorded in MP No.2/2017 is taken on record and considered in this Petition in support of claim of Petitioner. In this 
context Petitioner has filed documents in evidence which has been exhibited by witness WW1.The perusal of these

benefit from Respondent No.3 as per terms of contract Ex.W8, W9, and Ex. W12. Further, it is established that 
Petitioner was engaged for work by Respondent No. 3 i.e., Rishitha Associates for the period from 16.8.2009 to 
15.8.2012 to work in industry of R-1 Principal Employer Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Vishakpatnam Steel Plant. 

13. Although Respondent has contended that all the wages and dues towards the final settlement have been paid 
to the Petitioner workman but in support of his contention Respondent has not filed any document to corroborate it. 
Respondent No. 1 has also examined witness MW2 Sri K. Sudhakar Rao who has produced and exhibited document 
Ex.M1 to Ex.M6 and states that Ex. M6 is showing the amount paid by 20 Respondent to claimants but in cross 
examination MW? states that it is true that Ex.M6 relates to amount Rs. 28,58,522/- which is mentioned in para 5 of 
chief statement of MW1 and he is not aware that Rs. 61,76,628/- is still balance due to be paid to workman. Thus, the 
testimony of MW2 is not direct evidence in respect of payment of claimed amount in the petition, hence his evidence 
is not relevant in this regard. Therefore, contention of the Respondent No.1 in this context is untenable for the want 
of cogent and relevant evidence. Thus, on going oral and documentary evidence on record, it is established that the 
Petitioner workman is entitled to receive from the employer Respondent No.3 the amount of Rs.74,617.23ps. for the 
period of August,2009 to 2012 towards retrenchment allowances as per document Ex. W12. 

14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its 
industry during the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 as contract labour engaged by Respondent No.3. Since the 
Respondent No. 3 was sub-contractor for labour supply for the work order Ex. W8 of Respondent No.2, therefore, 
Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 2" 
Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the 
workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 


burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1! which he failed to 


2655 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 4, 2026/CHAITRA 14, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally. 

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)." In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 3% September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2656 


contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 


under the Act.” 

(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 47 February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 

(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 

“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 

16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 

16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for 
Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 


Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 


Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 


2657 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 4, 2026/CHAITRA 14, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. W8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 
The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 
2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 

whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 

(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 

(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 


of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 
Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 


Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 


16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (1५७) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 

(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 

Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 


definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 


[भाग I—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 4, 2026/चैत्र 14, 1948 2658 


the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1 industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable. 

18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 

ORDER 

The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 corresponding section 59 (2) under 
the Industrial Relation Code is allowed. 

Respondent No. | Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam is directed to pay the amount of Rs. 74,617.23ps. to the Petitioner within 30 days from the date of 
this order. Respondent No.1 is further directed to pay the interest @ 12% per annum on this amount from the date of 
due i.e., 16-08-2012 up to the date of payment. 

It is further directed that Respondent No.1 is entitled to recover the said amount paid to Petitioner from 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No. 3 the sub-contractor jointly and severally. 

Ordered accordingly.

The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. RLCP/8(21)/2023 dated 28/12/2023 
passed in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2A) of Section 10 of the 
Industrial Dispute Act 1947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as under: 
“Whether the action of the Managing Director, M/s. Pramerica Life Insurance Ltd, in terminating the 
services of Shri Ajay Dattaram More from 13.01.2023 is legal and justified? If not, to what relief the 
workman is entitled to? 
2. Whether the demand of the workman Shri Ajay Dattaram More for payment of salary and incentives along 
with back wages and all other consequential benefits is legal and justified? If yes, to what relief the workman 
is entitled to?” 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (1) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (I), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries vy. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; 


Since no statement of claim has been filed by the union in support of his case, the claim is liable to be dismissed. 
For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the union is not entitled for any relief. 
Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid. 


Award as above.

"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable

wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month."

14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its

workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 
burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and

includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 


Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 


powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not.

Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right,

with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 


during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of

AWARD 


In exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub —section (2A) of Section 10 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947),Government Of India through the Ministry of Labour, vide its Order 
No.L-41011/30/2002 -IR(B-I) dated 18/12/2002 has been pleased to refer the following dispute between the 
employer i.e. management of D.R.M. Eastern Railway, Mughalsarai Division and their workman through General 
Secretary, Gaya Railway Poldar Workers Union, Gaya for adjudication by this Tribunal: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the claim of Gaya Railway Station Poldar Workers Union for issuing identity card and 
treating them at par with the licensed porters by railway administration is legal and justified? if so, 
what relief the union is entitled to?”?” 


2. On receiving order no. L-41011/30/2002 -IR(B-I) dated 18/12/2002 Government of India, Ministry of Labour, 
New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, Reference case no. 09 of 2003 was registered on 01.01.2003 and thereafter 
the notices were sent to the parties with a direction to appear and submit their written statements along with relevant 
documents and witnesses in support of their claims. 


3. After service of notice, both parties appeared previously and filed their authorities, W/S and subsequently 
rejoinder. It further appears that on 22.09.2025 this case was reserved for award but in course of dictating judgement 
it transpired that hearing on behalf of the workman side is necessary and this case put up for argument of workman on 
01.12.2025 but workman failed to appear before this Tribunal and all notices returned back with endorsement 
“refused” as well as re-notice with endorsement “Addressee Left”. 


4. On perusal of the entire case record it transpires that workman/union has lost his interest in this case and 
therefore, for the ends of justice, this case deserves to be dismissed for non prosecution. 


5. Hence, 
ORDERED 


that this case is hereby dismissed for non prosecution and a “No Dispute Award” be drawn up in respect of the 
above reference case. Let the copies of Award in duplicate be sent to the Ministry of Labour & Employment, 
Government of India, New Delhi for information and notification.

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour & Employment vide its Order No. L-14011/15/2018-IR(DU) 
dated 27.11.2018 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Con..2 
The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether the action of the management of Indian Coast Guard, Base Maintenance Unit, Chennai, in 
transferring Sh. P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter to [CGS Mandapam in an non-existing post at ICGS 
Mandapam is legal and justified? If not, to what relief Sh. P.Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter is entitled 
to?” 


As per the claim statement the petitioner is an Indian Coast Guard Civilian Employees Union, registered under the 
Trade Union Act, 1926 was formed primarily to protect the interest of the workmen and for the welfare of the 
employees apart from maintaining harmonious relationship with the Management. It is submitted that there are 60 
civilian workmen in the establishment and most of them are members of the Union, this being the only union

functioning in the establishment to espouse the cause of the workmen. It is submitted that the Union raised an 
Industrial Dispute before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C) by letter dated 21.11.2017 under Section 2(K) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act,1947 over the issue relating to the unfair labour practices adopted by the respondent 
Management. It is submitted that the union was registered on 07.07.2017 vide Regn. No.508/TVR under the Trade 
Unions Act, 1947 and thereafter in the General Body Meeting the office bearers were elected. It is submitted that the 
fact relating to the registration of the union and the list of elected office bearers was communicated to the respondent 
Management by letter No.ICGEU/BMU/01/2017, dated 15.07.2017. 


2. It is submitted that the 1 respondent has framed the “Transfer Policy-Civilian” by letter no.CP/0518 dated 
22.11.2006 and circulated to the Regional Commanders for compliance. Para 4(c) deals with Group ‘B’ ‘C’ ‘D’ 
Non-Gazetted personal, wherein it is clearly stated that postings and transfer of these employees are to be kept at 
absolute minimum level keeping in view the administrative requirement and need for manning the posts at various 
stations. It has also been clearly mentioned that in case of transfers being inescapable, volunteers for the postings or 
transfer will be called. As far as possible only volunteers will be transferred to these vacancies. It has also been 
clearly stated that as far as possible the group ‘C’ and ‘D’ employee should not be transferred over long distance 
and efforts should be made to accommodate them near their choice station to the extent possible. 


3. As per the above, Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was elected as Treasurer of the union. Since the Respondent / 
Management was against the formation of the union, the employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was relieved and directed 
to report for duty at ICGS, Mandapam by letter No.CP/277/17, dated 31.10.2017 


4. The transfer order dated 20.10.2017 was not served on the workman till date. While the petitioner union requested 
that Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj be declared a protected workman, but the Management swiftly reacted by transferring 
Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj and victimized him by adopting unfair labour practice. Hence requested the following relief. 


i) To declare that the transfer order bearing no.1340 dated 20.10.2017 issued by the 37 Respondent 
transferring Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter from Basic Maintenance Unit, Chennai to Indian Coast 
Guard Station, Mandapam is not justified as per the guidelines laid down by the 1“ respondent in the Transfer 
Policy CP/0518 dated 22.11.2006 


ii) And to pass such other award/order as this Hon’ble Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour 
Court may deem fit and necessary in the circumstances of the case and thus render justice.

5. The respondent in its reply stated that the Indian Coast Guard Civilian Employees Union has not been recognized 
by the Ministry of Defence, as per CGHA letter WE/0302/Welfare dated 09.10.2019.The transfer order of the three 
(3) civilian personal was promulgated vide CGRHQ(E) letter 1340 dated 20.10.17. Accordingly, the individual was 
relieved from Basic Maintenance Unit, Chennai to report at Indian Coast Guard Station, Madapam as per the 
transfer policy and pleaded that the petition be dismissed as devoid of merit. 


6. The Respondent filed the following documents in support of their contention 


Exhibit No. Date Description 

Ex.M1 18.04.2018 Nature of duties carried out by Indian Coast Guard Base 
Maintenance Unit (Chennai) 

Ex.M2 09.10.2019 Service Association and Welfare in Indian Coast Guard 

Ex.M3 22.11.2006 Transfer Policy - Civilians 


7. Heard both learned counsel and perused the records. The point arised for determination is whether the transfer of 
Shri P. Ayan Aurl Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter as ICGS, Mandapam is an not existing post at ICGS, Mandapam is legal 
and justify? If not, what relief is Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar fitter is entitled to? 


8. The claimant in its claim statement stated that the following points regarding the transfer policy. 


(a) Posting and transfer are to be kept at the absolute minimum level 
(b) Volunteers for the postings of the transfer called and will be transferred 
(c) Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ employees should not be transferred over long distance 


9. In petition claim the hardships caused to transferring described as under 


(a) Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was transferred during October,2017 quite impossible for getting admission for his 
school going children at the new station 

(b) The workman unable to shift his family in the midst of the academic year 

(c) The employee kept the family in Chennai for his child to complete the studies in the academic year but the 
Estate Office, CPWD directed him to vacate the quarters and threatened to impose a penalty 

(d) The employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj fell sick because of the mental agony and remains on leave on medical 
ground from 1.11.2017 to 28.6.2018 

(e) When the workman reported for duty on 29.06.2018 at the Mandapam station, the 31 Respondent directed 


him to report for duty in Chennai for four days in a week. 


10. On perusal of whole the claim statement, the claimant nowhere stated that Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was transferred 
to a non-existing post at ICGS Mandapam. On perusal of the claim statement, it appears that the Respondent did not 
violate the transfer policy, as the Mandapam station is not far away from Chennai station. 


11. It is the fundamental duty of transferring employee to seek the permission to overstay at Govt. accommodation by 
mentioning the sufficient reasons for occupation of the allotted house. In claim petition this facts nowhere mention 
that any application mentioning sufficient reasons for over staying at the allotted house was made or not. In this 
situation it can be presumed that no application was made by the transferring employee to the authority. 
Transferring employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj fails to submit the medical certificates which might have established 
the genuine grounds of his absence due to medical reasons. 


12. It is stated in the claim petition that the employee was transferred due to his involvement in the union, but the 
claimant fails to submit any evidence that may establish this fact that respondent had showed its jealous against the 
employee. The only vague reason given is that he was an elected as an office bearer in the union, the transfer of an 
employee do not appear as a result of his election to the union. 


13. The claimant has stated that no transfer order was provided to the transferred employee and that only a relieving 
order was provided to the transferee employee. The relieving order issued to Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj dated 
31.10.2017 is available at page no.2 of the paper book in this document, it is mentioned clearly that the Competent 
Authority has approved the transfer of Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj with a direction to report at ICGS Mandapam by 
10.11.2017. The relieving order was issued by the Section Officer in compliance with the order passed by the 
Competent Authority hence, no right of the transfree employee was violated by not providing a separate transfer 
order. 


14. As per the discussion above, the transfer order was not made by the Respondent in violation of transfer policy or 
against the non-existing post, it also not proved that this order was made due to desirous wish of the respondent. 


AWARD 
The claim petition filed by the Petitioner union is dismissed. The reference is answered accordingly.

By order No. L-12011/17/2022-IR(B-D) dated: 02.06.2022 the present industrial dispute has been referred 
for adjudication to this CGIT, Lucknow, in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub- 
section (2A) of Section 10 the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) by the Central Government, with following 
schedule: 


"Whether the demand of All India Ex Servicemen Bank Employees' Federation with regard to allowing 2 
years weightage to the ex-servicemen while promoting from sub-staff to clerical cadre & Clerical to Officer 
is justified? If yes, what relief the workman is entitled to?" 


Accordingly, an industrial dispute No. 31/2022 has been registered. 
On 24.04.2023 claimant filed claim statement has been filed with following relief: 


“(i) Modification in 02 Yrs Weightage in Promotion circular in Baroda UP Bank be Expunged from its 
circular. 


(ii) Govt policy letter no. 02/8/78-SCT (B) dated 28th January, 1983 and further F. No. 10/49/84-SCT (B) 
dated 13th Aug 1986 be implemented in letter and spirit in Baroda UP Bank. 


(iii) Weightage of all candidates who lost the opportunity of 02 Years be re-stored till they actually avail the 
opportunity along with Shri sanjeev Mandal. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 9, 2026/वैशाख 19, 1948 4063 


(iv) Weightage to Ex-Serviceman, who could not succeed in the in promotion exam or could not actually 
avails the opportunity due to any reason/exigencies, their chances be retained as unused for future 
promotion examination.” 


On behalf of the respondent statement of defense filed on 08.10.2023 denying claim of the workman; wherein 
preliminary objection has been taken by the respondent. 


Thereafter, workman filed rejoinder on 04.04.2025 and evidence on affidavit in support of his statement of claim on 
26.05.2025. 


However, from the perusal of record, it is clearly established that claimant/workman did not turn up for cross- 
examination in spite of several opportunities; and it is a case of no evidence from the side of workman/claimant in 
support of his case. 


Thus, in view of the above said facts and the law as laid by the Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries 
v. Labour Court (1) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove 
illegality of the order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. 
Whenever a workman raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative 
for him to file written statement before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is 
challenged and he must also produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file 
written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred by the State Government cannot be answered in 
favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (I), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., 
V.K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) 
FLR 38 and Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led 
by or on behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In 
such a situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead 
evidence to establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, 
who would fail if no evidence is led.”’ 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. 
A perusal of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led 
by the respondent. In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


As the claimant/workman did not turn up for cross-examination, so it is a case of no evidence filed on behalf of 
workman in support of case, liable to be dismissed. 


For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and; and the workman is not entitled for any relief. 
Award as above. 
Lucknow.

After hearing the parties/their legal representative and Advocate, the first point to be considered the point to be 
consider in the present case:- 


A). whether the reference dated 17.02.2015, is vague and on the basis of the same no cause of action arises on the 
part of workman/claimant to file present claim petition. 


In order to decide the said dispute it would be appropriate to go through Section 10 of the Industrial Dispute Act. 
10. Section 10 of Industrial Disputes Act reads thus: 


"10. Reference of disputes to Boards, Courts or Tribunals. (1) [Where the appropriate Government is of 
opinion that any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended, it may at any time), by order in writing,- 


(a) refer the dispute to a Board for promoting a settlement thereof; or 
(b) refer any matter appearing to be connected with or relevant to the dispute to a Court for inquiry; or 


[(c) refer the dispute or any matter appearing to be connected with, or relevant to, the dispute, if it relates to 
any matter specified in the Second Schedule, to a Labour Court for adjudication; or 


(d) refer the dispute or any matter appearing to be connected with, or relevant to, the dispute, whether it 
relates to any matter specified in the Second Schedule or the Third Schedule, to a Tribunal for adjudication: 


Provided that where the dispute relates to any matter specified in the Third Schedule and is not likely to 
affect more than one hundred workmen, the appropriate Government may, if it so thinks fit, make the 
reference to a Labour Court under clause (c):]" 


11. Plain reading of aforesaid provision would show that when industrial dispute exists or is apprehended, appropriate 
Government can refer dispute to Court for enquiry or if relates to any matter specified in Second Schedule to Labour 
Court for adjudication or make Reference to Tribunal, if dispute relates to matters specified in Second Schedule or 
Third Schedule. It is, therefore, obvious that Reference can be made only when industrial disputes exists or is 
apprehended by Competent Authority. 


13. The aforesaid legal position would make explicit that existence of industrial dispute is a paramount and important 
consideration while dealing with Reference. 


Only existent or apprehended industrial disputes can be referred for consideration of Court or Tribunal. However, at 
the time of taking decision whether Reference to be made or not, appropriate Government need not venture into

merits of dispute, as making Reference is only administrative function. Only because Reference is made under 
Section 10(1), Court or Tribunal is not precluded from entering into aspects of delay and laches or to record findings 
as to existence or non-existence of dispute. 


In case of Prabhakar v. Joint Director, Sericulture Department and "another, 2015 (147) FLR 341 (SC), the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court considered and held the impact of delay and laches in Reference made under Section 10(1) of 
Industrial Disputes Act and observed in paragraph No. 14 as under: 


"40. An industrial dispute has to be referred by the appropriate Government for adjudication and the 
workman cannot approach the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal directly, except in those cases which are 
covered by Section 2-A of the Act. Reference is made under Section 10 of the Act in those cases where the 
appropriate Government forms an opinion that ‘any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended’. The words 
‘industrial dispute exists' are of paramount importance unless there is an existence of an industrial dispute 
(or the dispute is apprehended or it is apprehended such a dispute may arise in near future), no reference is 
to be made. Thus, existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute is a sine qua non for making the 
reference. No doubt, at the time of taking a decision whether a reference is to be made or not, the 
appropriate Government is not to go into the merits of the dispute. Making of reference is only an 
administrative function. At the same time, on the basis of material on record, satisfaction of the existence of 
the industrial dispute or the apprehension of an industrial dispute is necessary. Such existence/apprehension 
of industrial dispute, thus, becomes a condition precedent, though it will be only subjective satisfaction 
based on material on record. Since, we are not concerned with the satisfaction dealing with cases where 
there is apprehended industrial dispute, discussion that follows would confine to existence of an industrial 
dispute. Dispute or difference arises when one party make a demand and other party rejects the same. It is 
held by this Court in number of cases that before raising the industrial dispute making of demand is a 
necessary pre-condition. In such a scenario, if the services of a workman are terminated and he does not 
make the demand and/or raise the issue alleging wrongful termination immediately thereafter or within 
reasonable time and raises the same after considerable lapse of period, whether it can be said that industrial 
dispute still exist. Since there is no period of limitation, it gives right to the workman to raise the dispute 
even belatedly. However, if the dispute is raised after a long period, it has to be seen as to whether such a 
dispute still exists? Thus, notwithstanding the fact that law of limitation does not apply, it is to be shown by 
the workman that there is a dispute in praesenti. For this purpose, he has to demonstrate that even if 
considerable period has lapsed and there are laches and delays, such delay has not resulted into making the 
industrial dispute seized to exist. Therefore, if the workman is able to give satisfactory explanation for these 
laches and delays and demonstrate that the circumstances discloses that issue is still alive, delay would not 
come in his way because of the reason that law of limitation has no application. On the other hand, if 
because of such delay dispute no longer remains alive and is to be treated as "dead", then it would be non- 
existent dispute which cannot be referred." 


Thus it can be held on the point in issue that for raising industrial dispute demand is precondition. In case, employee 
fails to make demand, dispute cannot be referred.
